source_text: Vae, ait, per quem traditur filius hominis. ergo iam \'uae* constat imprecationis et comminationis inclamationem intellegendam et irato et offenso deputandam, nisi si ludas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus. at si impune, uacat \'uae\'; si non impune, utique ab eo puniendus, in quem scelus traditionis admisit. porro si sciens passus est hominem, quem ipse comitatui suo adsciuerat, in tantum scelus ruere, noli iam de creatore circa Adam retractare quae in tuum quoque deum retorquentur: aut ignorasse illum, qui non ex prouidentia obstitit peccaturo, aut obsistere non potuisse, si (non) ignorabat, aut noluisse, si et sciebat et poterat, atque ita malitiosum iudicandum, qui passus sit hominem suum ex delicto perire. suadeo igitur agnoscas potius et in isto creatorem quam parem illi deum optimum aduersus sententiam tuam facias. nam et Petrum praesumptorie aliquid elocutum negationi potius destinando zeloten deum tibi ostendit. debuit etiam osculo tradi, propheticus scilicet Christus, ut eius scilicet filius, qui labiis a populo diligebatur. Perductus in consessum, an ipse esset Christus, interrogatur. de quo Christo Iudaei quaesissent nisi de suo? cur ergo non uel tunc alium eis prodidit? \'ut pati posset\', inquis, id est, ut ille optimus ignorantes adhuc in scelus mergeret. atquin et si dixisset, passurus esset. si dixero enim, inquit, uobis, non credetis. porro non credituri perseuerassent in necem eius. et cur non magis passurus esset, si alterius dei ac per hoc aduersarium creatoris (se) manifestasset? ergo non, ut pateretur, alium se tunc quoque supersedit ostendere, sed quoniam ex ore eius confessionem extorquere cupiebant, nec confesso tamen credituri, qui eum ex operibus scripturas adimplentibus agnouisse debuerant. ita eius fuit occultasse se, cui ultro debebatur agnitio. et tamen adhuc eis manum porrigens: abhinc, inquit, erit filius hominis sedens ad dexteram uirtutis dei. suggerebat enim se esse (de) Danihelis prophetia (filium hominis* et de psalmo Dauid (sedentem ad dexteram dei\'. itaque ex isto dicto et scripturae comparatione inluminati, quem se uellet intellegi: ergo, inquiunt, tu dei filius es? cuius dei, nisi quem solum nouerant? cuius dei, nisi quem in psalmo meminerant dixisse filio suo: sede ad dexteram meam? <sed respondit: uos dicitis, quasi: non ego\\ atquin confirmauit id se esse, quod illi dixerant, dum rursus interrogant. unde autem probabis interrogatiuo et non (et) ipsos confirmatiuo pronuntiasse: ergo tu filius dei es, ut, quia oblique ostenderat se per scripturas filium dei intellegendum, sic senserint: \'ergo tu dei es filius\', quod te non uis aperte dicere? atque ita et ille (uos dicitis\' confirmatiue respondit, et adeo sic fuit pronuntiatio eius, ut perseuerauerint in eo, quod pronuntiatio sapiebat.
pass_a_gloss: Woe, he says, to him through whom the Son of Man is betrayed. Therefore, it is already clear that this 'woe' is to be understood as an exclamation of imprecation and commination, and to be attributed to one who is angry and offended, unless he who was about to relate such a great crime was doing so with impunity. But if with impunity, then 'woe' is unnecessary; if not with impunity, then he is certainly to be punished by him into whom the crime of betrayal was admitted. Furthermore, if he knowingly allowed the man, whom he himself had added to his company, to rush into such a great crime, do not now retract concerning the Creator in the case of Adam what can also be retorted against your own god: either he was ignorant, because he did not prevent the one who was about to sin, or he was unable to prevent it, if he was not ignorant, or he was unwilling, if he both knew and was able, and thus is to be judged malicious, who allowed his man to perish because of a fault. I advise, therefore, that you rather acknowledge the Creator in this case, and make him, who is the best God, contrary to your opinion. For even Peter, who had spoken something presumptuously, shows a zealous God to you by destined denial. He ought to have been betrayed even with a kiss, the prophetic Christ, so that he, the Son, who was loved by the people with their lips, might be known. Brought into the council, he is asked if he himself is the Christ. Concerning which Christ the Jews would have asked, unless it was about their own? Why, therefore, did he not betray another to them at that time? 'So that he might suffer,' you say, that is, so that he might plunge the ignorant into sin. But even if he had said it, he would have suffered. For if I say, he says, you will not believe. Furthermore, those who were not going to believe would have persevered in his death. And why was he not going to suffer even more, if he had manifested himself as the God of another and thus as the adversary of the Creator? Therefore, it was not so that he might suffer that he showed himself to be another at that time, but because they wanted to extort a confession from his mouth, and yet they would not have believed even if he had confessed, who ought to have recognized him from his works, which fulfilled the scriptures. Thus, it was his to hide himself, to whom recognition was owed even spontaneously. And yet, he was still stretching out his hand to them: 'From now on,' he says, 'the Son of Man will be sitting at the right hand of the power of God.' For he was suggesting that he was the one from Daniel's prophecy, the Son of Man, and from David's psalm, the one sitting at the right hand of God. And so, from this statement and the comparison of scripture, they were enlightened, whom he wanted to be understood: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God?' Whose God, unless the one they alone knew? Whose God, unless the one they remembered from the psalm, who said to his Son: 'Sit at my right hand?' But he responded: 'You say so,' as if to say: 'not I.' And yet, he confirmed that he was what they had said, while they were asking again. Whence, however, will you prove that he spoke interrogatively and not also confirmatively, when they said: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God,' so that, because he had shown himself obliquely through the scriptures to be the Son of God, they thus perceived: 'Therefore, you are the Son of God,' which you do not want to say openly? And so, he also responded confirmatively with 'You say so,' and thus his pronouncement was such that they persevered in what his pronouncement implied.

choices.why: indicating the means by which the Son of Man is betrayed
indicating that God knowingly allowed the man to rush into sin
indicating that God is to be judged malicious for allowing his man to perish

pass_b_english: "Woe," he says, "to the one through whom the Son of Man is betrayed." So it is already clear that this 'woe' must be understood as an outcry of imprecation and threat, and attributed to one who is angry and offended—unless the one about to report such a monstrous crime was doing so with impunity. But if with impunity, then 'woe' is superfluous; if not with impunity, then the man is certainly to be punished by the very one into whom the crime of betrayal entered. Furthermore, if he knowingly let the man, whom he himself had added to his company, rush into such a monstrous crime, do not now revisit the Creator's case regarding Adam in arguments that rebound against your own god: either he was ignorant, because he did not prevent the one about to sin from doing so, or he was unable to prevent it, if he was not ignorant, or he was unwilling, if he both knew and was able—and thus is to be judged malicious, since he let his man perish because of a fault. I advise you, therefore, to rather acknowledge the Creator in this instance, instead of making a god equal to him, the best God, contrary to your opinion. For even Peter, who had spoken presumptuously, shows you a zealous God by destining him for denial. He ought to have been betrayed even with a kiss, the prophetic Christ, so that he—the Son, whom the people loved with their lips—might be recognized. Brought before the council, he is asked whether he himself is the Christ. About which Christ would the Jews have asked, if not their own? Why, then, did he not betray another to them at that time? "So that he might suffer," you say—that is, so that he might plunge the ignorant into sin. But even if he had said it, he would have suffered. "For if I tell you," he says, "you will not believe." Moreover, those who were not going to believe would have persisted in killing him. And why would he not have suffered even more, if he had revealed himself as another's god and thus the Creator's adversary? Therefore, it was not so that he might suffer that he refrained from showing himself to be another at that time, but because they wanted to extort a confession from his mouth, and yet they would not have believed even if he had confessed—those who ought to have recognized him from his works, which fulfilled the scriptures. Thus it fell to him to hide himself, to whom recognition was owed even spontaneously. And yet he still held out his hand to them: "From now on," he says, "the Son of Man will be sitting at the right hand of the power of God." For he was indicating that he was the one from Daniel's prophecy, the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13), and from David's psalm, the one sitting at the right hand of God (Psalm 110:1). And so, enlightened by this statement and the comparison of scripture, they grasped whom he wanted to be understood: "Therefore, you are the Son of God?" Whose God, unless the only one they knew? Whose God, unless the one they remembered from the psalm, who said to his Son: "Sit at my right hand"? But he responded: "You say so," as if to say: "Not I." And yet he confirmed that he was what they had said, while they were asking again. How, however, will you prove that he spoke interrogatively and not also confirmatively, when they said: "Therefore, you are the Son of God," so that, because he had shown himself obliquely through the scriptures to be the Son of God, they thus perceived: "Therefore, you are the Son of God"—which you do not want to say openly? And so he also responded confirmatively with "You say so," and his pronouncement was such that they persisted in what his pronouncement implied.
